name: Acute Viral Hepatitis

likely: Hepatitis B virus (if relevant risk factors: injection drug use, unsafe transfusion, vertical transmission)
possible: Hepatitis C virus (less commonly causes acute icteric illness)
Other hepatotropic viruses (CMV, EBV) in atypical presentations
pathogens.why: In endemic settings with fecal-oral transmission risk (contaminated food/water), Hepatitis A and E are the dominant causes of acute viral hepatitis, with Hepatitis E of particular concern in pregnancy due to higher fulminant hepatic failure risk. Hepatitis B should be specifically considered with parenteral/sexual risk factors, since management and chronicity implications differ substantially.

investigations.why: Marked transaminase elevation (often >10x upper limit of normal) with hyperbilirubinemia is characteristic of acute viral hepatitis and helps distinguish it from other causes of jaundice.

investigations.test: Hepatitis A IgM, Hepatitis E IgM
investigations.why: Confirms the most likely causes in this setting; both are the standard first-line serologic tests for acute fecal-oral hepatitis.

investigations.test: Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), IgM anti-HBc
investigations.why: Identifies acute Hepatitis B, which has different counseling, monitoring, and contact-tracing/vaccination implications than A or E.
A rising INR is the key early warning sign of evolving acute liver failure and should be tracked closely.
Screens for hepatic encephalopathy, the clinical hallmark of progression to acute liver failure requiring urgent escalation of care.

reason: Jaundice with nausea/vomiting and constitutional symptoms, particularly following exposure to potentially contaminated food or water, is consistent with acute viral hepatitis (commonly Hepatitis A or E in this setting). This is a viral infection — antibiotics have no role and management is supportive (rest, hydration, avoidance of hepatotoxic drugs and alcohol), with monitoring for the rare progression to acute liver failure.
